Existence and instability of steady states for a triangular cross-diffusion system: a computer-assisted proof

Maxime Breden ††thanks: CMLA, ENS Cachan, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, 61 avenue du Président Wilson, 94230 Cachan, France & Département de Mathématiques et de Statistique, Université Laval, 1045 avenue de la Médecine, Québec, QC, G1V 0A6, Canada. maxime.breden@ens-cachan.fr    Roberto Castelli ††thanks: VU University Amsterdam, Department of Mathematics, De Boelelaan 1081, 1081 HV Amsterdam, The Netherlands. r.castelli@vu.nl
Abstract

In this paper, we present and apply a computer-assisted method to study steady states of a triangular cross-diffusion system. Our approach consist in an a posteriori validation procedure, that is based on using a fixed point argument around a numerically computed solution, in the spirit of the Newton-Kantorovich theorem. It allows us to prove the existence of various non homogeneous steady states for different parameter values. In some situations, we get as many as 13 coexisting steady states. We also apply the a posteriori validation procedure to study the linear stability of the obtained steady states, proving that many of them are in fact unstable.

Key words Rigorous numerics ⋅\cdot Cross-diffusion ⋅\cdot Steady states
Eigenvalue problem ⋅\cdot Spectral analysis ⋅\cdot Fixed point argument

2010 AMS Subject Classification 35K59 ⋅\cdot 35Q92 ⋅\cdot 65G20 ⋅\cdot 65N35

1 Introduction

The primary goal of describing physical systems with mathematical models is to be able to explain and predict natural phenomena, within some range of approximation. In some circumstances the mathematical prediction and the experimental evidence don’t agree, and a more trustful model is then required. Typically, one can add nonlinear or non homogeneous terms to get a more refined model, but this often seriously complicates the mathematical analysis of the system, which can become very hard, if not impossible, to study analytically. In this situation, numerical simulations allow insight of the phenomena and provide approximate, often very accurate, solutions. Aiming at formulating theorems, a powerful tool to validate approximate solutions into rigorous mathematical statements is provided by the rigorous computational techniques.

The diffusive Lotka-Volterra system, a well known model for population dynamics to study the competition between two species, is paradigmatic of the situation discussed above. It consists in the system

{∂u∂t=d1Δu+(r1−a1u−b1v)u,on ​ℝ+×Ω,∂v∂t=d2Δv+(r2−b2u−a2v)v,on ​ℝ+×Ω,∂u∂n=0=∂v∂n,on ​ℝ+×∂Ω,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u+(r_{1}-a_{1}u-b_{1}v)u,\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v+(r_{2}-b_{2}u-a_{2}v)v,\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=0=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n},\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (1)

where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}, and u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x)≥0u(t,x),v(t,x)\geq 0 represent the population densities of two species at time tt and position xx. The non negative coefficients did_{i}, rir_{i}, aia_{i} and bib_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) describe the diffusion, the unhindered growth of the species, the intra-specific competition and the inter-specific competition respectively.

One of the fundamental problems is to determine if and under which assumptions the two species coexist, that converts into proving the existence or non-existence of stable positive equilibrium solutions. Several works has been produced to classify and analyse the stability of the equilibria for (1) and of related systems. We refer for instance to [38] for a short review. Of particular interest for our discussion is the result presented in [31]. If the domain Ω\Omega is convex, in that paper it is proved that any spatially non-constant equilibrium solution of (1) is unstable, if it exists. This implies that if the two species coexist, their densities must be homogeneous in the whole domain.

However, biological observations suggest that two competing species could coexist by forming pattern to avoid each other (a phenomenom called spatial segregation). Therefore we would like the model to exhibit stable non homogeneous steady states, but the quoted result shows that this is excluded (at least for convex domains). We point out that stable non homogeneous equilibria have been shown to exist for non convex domains [36], or for systems involving more than two species [30].

In the case of two competing species, to account for the expected stable inhomogeneous steady sates, a generalization of (1) was proposed in [47]:

{∂u∂t=Δ⁡((d1+d12​v)​u)+(r1−a1​u−b1​v)​u,on ​ℝ+×Ω,∂v∂t=Δ⁡((d2+d21​u)​v)+(r2−b2​u−a2​v)​v,on ​ℝ+×Ω,∂u∂n=0=∂v∂n,on ​ℝ+×∂Ω,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta((d_{1}+d_{12}v)u)+(r_{1}-a_{1}u-b_{1}v)u,\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta((d_{2}+d_{21}u)v)+(r_{2}-b_{2}u-a_{2}v)v,\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=0=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n},\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (2)

where the added cross-diffusion terms Δ⁡(u​v)\Delta(uv) model that the two species try to avoid each other, by diffusing more when more individuals of the other species are present.

Since its introduction the system (2) has been studied extensively, one of the main reason being that it seems to exhibit a much wider variety of steady states than (1), especially non homogeneous ones, in accordance to laboratory experiments. Several numerical studies have been presented, displaying intricate bifurcation diagrams of steady states (see for instance [26, 27] and also Figure 1). Consider for instance the homogenous equilibria

(ue​q,ve​q):=(r1​a2−r2​b1a1​a2−b1​b2,r2​a1−r1​b2a1​a2−b1​b2)(u_{eq},v_{eq}):=\left(\frac{r_{1}a_{2}-r_{2}b_{1}}{a_{1}a_{2}-b_{1}b_{2}},\frac{r_{2}a_{1}-r_{1}b_{2}}{a_{1}a_{2}-b_{1}b_{2}}\right) (3)

in the strong intra-specific case, i.e. when b1a2<r1r2<a1b2\frac{b_{1}}{a_{2}}<\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}<\frac{a_{1}}{b_{2}} (the other case a1b2<r1r2<b1a2\frac{a_{1}}{b_{2}}<\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}<\frac{b_{1}}{a_{2}} is known as the strong inter-specific competition case). While (ue​q,ve​q)(u_{eq},v_{eq}) is stable for (1) for any diffusion coefficient d1,d2≥0d_{1},d_{2}\geq 0, adding strong enough cross-diffusion can destabilize this equilibria, from which new non homogeneous steady states can bifurcate. A link between this cross-diffusion induced instability and the standard Turing instability for reaction-diffusion systems is made in [26].

While from one side the addition of these nonlinear cross-diffusion terms yields a more reliable model, on the other it seriously complicates the analytical treatment of the system. Even the existence of global classical solutions of (2) (completed with non negative initial data) is a challenging question that is still fairly open. Local in time existence can be obtained by the theory of quasilinear parabolic systems [1], but to then get bounds that prevent blowups requires restrictions on the coefficients, as for instance d21=0d_{21}=0 [17]. In this particular case, sometimes called triangular cross-diffusion system, some recent progresses were also made in [20] by combining entropy methods with a 3 component reaction-diffusion system without cross-diffusion (first introduced in [26]), that is used to approach (2). Entropy methods were also used to improve upon the existing results for the full cross-diffusion system, see [28, 19] and the references therein.

Existence and stability results for non homogeneous steady states of (2) have also been established following different approaches including bifurcations techniques [39], singular perturbation techniques [40, 35] and fixed point index theory [46]. Because of the presence of the cross-diffusion term, the analytical studies are limited to those solutions that are either close the homogeneous steady states, or in very specific parameter ranges. However, the numerically computed bifurcation diagram reveals a very rich structure that includes coexistence of many different steady states for a given set of parameter values, as well as secondary bifurcations. To the best of the author’s knowledge, even the existence of these solutions is not yet proved and it seems out of reach of purely analytical techniques.

The aim of this paper is to prove existence and study the linear stability of several non-homogenous steady states of (2), significantly far from being perturbations of the homogeneous equilibria, also showing multiplicity of solutions for the same set of parameters. The kind of technique adopted here is often referred to as validated numerics, because the goal is to prove the existence of a genuine solution of the problem in a sharp and explicit neighborhood of a numerical one, hence, in this sense, to validate the approximate solution (more details in Section 2). More precisely, we follow the so called radii polynomial approach, a quite general technique based on the contraction mapping argument that has been adapted to solve several differential problems in areas ranging from dynamical systems to ordinary and partial differential equations through delay differential equation and chaotic dynamics. This is the first time that rigorous computational techniques are applied to PDE system with cross interactions in the leading differential operator. The cross-diffusion terms are indeed a major technical hurdles, since they enfeeble the smoothing effect of the higher order differential operator.

In this work we restrict ourself to the triangular case and assume that the space dimension is 1 (i.e. we fix d21=0d_{21}=0 and Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1)). The method can easily be extended to higher space dimension (say 2 or 3), but of course the computational cost would increase. The generalization to a full cross-diffusion system is less straightforward. Indeed, as mentioned above, it will become apparent in the next sections that the cross-diffusion structure hinders the use of our validation method, and that we take advantage of the triangular configuration to overcome this difficulty.

The system we are dealing with is the following:

{((d1+d12v)u)′′+(r1−a1u−b1v)u=0,on ​(0,1),d2v′′+(r2−b2u−a2v)v=0,on ​(0,1),u′​(0)=u′​(1)=0,v′​(0)=v′​(1)=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\!\left((d_{1}+d_{12}v)u\right)^{\prime\prime}+(r_{1}-a_{1}u-b_{1}v)u=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &d_{2}v^{\prime\prime}+(r_{2}-b_{2}u-a_{2}v)v=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &u^{\prime}(0)=u^{\prime}(1)=0,\\ &v^{\prime}(0)=v^{\prime}(1)=0.\end{aligned}\right. (4)

Figure 1 depicts a bifurcation diagram of solutions of (4), with given values for the parameters rir_{i}, aia_{i}, bib_{i} and d12d_{12}. This diagram was first obtained numerically in [26], using a 3-component system without cross-diffusion that approaches (4). We point out that even in the somewhat restricted framework with Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1) and d12=0d_{12}=0, the steady states of (2) already manifest very complex and interesting behavior when the parameters vary.

The first result concerns the existence of steady states.

Theorem 1.1.

Referring to Figure 2, each bullet represents a solution of (4), for the parameter values r1=5r_{1}=5, r2=2r_{2}=2, a1=3a_{1}=3, a2=3a_{2}=3, b1=1b_{1}=1, b2=1b_{2}=1, d12=3d_{12}=3, and d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d. In particular there exists at least 13 different solutions when d1=d2=0.005d_{1}=d_{2}=0.005.

The proof of each steady states also provides precise qualitative informations about the solution, in terms of explicit bounds of the distance (in some function space, see Section 4) between the genuine solution that is proved to exist and a numerically computed approximation (more details in Section 5).

In [26], the linear stability of the obtained steady states was also studied (still numerically), suggesting that most of the solutions displayed in the bifurcation diagram of Figure 2 are unstable, while others seems to be stable. In this direction, the second contribution of this paper is a rigorous computational approach to the study of the spectral properties of the equilibria presented above.

Theorem 1.2.

Referring to Figure 3, each blue bullet represents an unstable steady state. Out of the 13 solutions at parameter value d=0.005d=0.005, at least 11 are unstable.

The steady states marked in red in Figure 3 and in particular the two solutions out of 13 that are not concerned by the above Theorem seem to be stable. However, at the moment we are not yet able to use our validation method to prove linear stability, as this requires to control the whole spectrum and not just a single eigenvalue. Still, we point out that the straight line of solutions at v⁡(0)=0.125v(0)=0.125 corresponds to the homogeneous steady state (3), for which the linear stability could of course be studied analytically. In particular it could be proven that, before the bifurcation occuring at d≃0.0328d\simeq 0.0328 the homogeneous steady state is linearly stable. Validated numerics techniques were used successfully to prove stability in other situations ([11, 29], see also [41]), but the adaptation to our problem presents several challenges (mainly due to the cross-diffusion terms, which muddle the asymptotic structure of the eigenvalue problem, see Section 6) and will be the object of future investigations.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we give a brief exposition of the validated numerics techniques we apply in this work, as well as additional references on the subject. In particular we state the Theorem 2.1, that serves as common reference and guideline for both the rigorous computation of the steady states and the rigorous enclosure of the eigenvalues. Section 3 is devoted to the introduction of some notations and elementary estimates that are used throughout the paper. In Sections 4 to 5, we then prove the existence of steady states. More precisely, in Section 4.1 we expose how to reformulate the problem of existence of solutions of (4) into a framework suitable for Theorem 2.1. In Section 4.3, we then derive explicit and implementable formulas for the bounds involved in Theorem 2.1, and finally give examples of results in Section 5. Sections 6 to 7 are dedicated to proving the instability of some of these steady states, following the same procedure: suitable reformulation in Section 6.1, bounds in Section 6.3 and results in Section 7.

2 Overview of the rigorous computational method

In this section we briefly explain the strategy for both solving (4) and computing the linear stability of the steady states by means of validated numerics techniques. Each problem is formulated as solving an equation F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 defined on a suitable Banach space. The core of the method, first presented in [49], consists in the introduction of an operator TT whose fixed points are in one-to-one correspondence with the zeros of F⁡(X)F(X). The existence and enclosure of the solution follow by the Banach fixed point theorem once the operator TT is proven to be a contraction on some complete set. The explicit determination of the neighborhood on which the operator is a contraction is done efficiently using the radii polynomial approach (see [18]), which is reminiscent of the Newton-Kantorovich Theorem. The technique can be summarized in the following statement.

Theorem 2.1.

Let (𝒳,‖⋅‖𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathcal{X}}), (𝒴,‖⋅‖𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathcal{Y}}) be Banach spaces and F:𝒳→𝒴F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} function. Let A:𝒴→𝒳A:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X} and A†:𝒳→𝒴A^{{\dagger}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} be linear operators, so that A​FAF maps 𝒳\mathcal{X} into itself. Let X¯∈𝒳\bar{X}\in\mathcal{X} and assume there exist positive constants YY, Z0Z_{0}, Z1Z_{1} and a positive function r↦Z2​(r)r\mapsto Z_{2}(r) such that

‖A​F​(X¯)‖𝒳\displaystyle\left\|AF(\bar{X})\right\|_{\mathcal{X}} ≤Y\displaystyle\leq Y (5)
\VERT​I−A​A†​\VERT𝒳\displaystyle\left\VERT I-AA^{{\dagger}}\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}} ≤Z0\displaystyle\leq Z_{0} (6)
\VERT​A​(D​F​(X¯)−A†)​\VERT𝒳\displaystyle\left\VERT A\left(DF(\bar{X})-A^{{\dagger}}\right)\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}} ≤Z1\displaystyle\leq Z_{1} (7)
\VERT​A​(D​F​(X)−D​F​(X¯))​\VERT𝒳\displaystyle\left\VERT A\left(DF(X)-DF(\bar{X})\right)\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}} ≤r​Z2​(r)∀X∈ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r),\displaystyle\leq rZ_{2}(r)\quad\forall~X\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r), (8)

where ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r) is the closed ball of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, centered at X¯\bar{X} and of radius rr, and \VERT⋅\VERT𝒳\VERT\cdot\VERT_{\mathcal{X}} denotes the operator norm on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Define the function PP as

P⁡(r)=Z2​(r)​r2−(1−(Z0+Z1))​r+Y.P(r)=Z_{2}(r)r^{2}-\left(1-(Z_{0}+Z_{1})\right)r+Y. (9)

If there exists r>0r>0 such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0, then the operator T:𝒳→𝒳T:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X} defined as

T=I−A​FT=I-AF (10)

has a unique fixed point in ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r). Moreover if AA is injective, then FF has a unique zero in ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r).

We omit the proof of the theorem, that can be found for instance in [18]. Nevertheless, in the next remark we explain the role of the different operators involved in the theorem and some instructions on how to define them. These considerations are detailed and made more explicit in Section 4.3 (resp. Section 6.3), where we derive the bounds YY, Z0Z_{0}, Z1Z_{1} and Z2​(r)Z_{2}(r) for an FF associated to the existence of solutions of (4) (resp. their instability). We also mention that in practice, because of the way we define AA, its injectivity is in fact implied by the existence of a r>0r>0 such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 (see Proposition 4.5).

Remark 2.2.
  • •

    X¯\bar{X} is chosen as an approximate solution for F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0, to be computed numerically as zero for a finite dimensional approximation of FF. The constant YY is the defect bound and measures how far is X¯\bar{X} from being a fixed point of TT. Depending on the accuracy of the approximate solution X¯\bar{X}, we expect YY to be small.

  • •

    The Zi​(r)Z_{i}(r), i=0,1,2i=0,1,2, are meant as bounds for the rate of contraction of the operator TT in the ball ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r). More precisely, Z0+Z1Z_{0}+Z_{1} provides a bound for the derivative of TT at X¯\bar{X}, while Z2​(r)Z_{2}(r) gives a correction for the derivative in the whole ball ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r). Assume for a moment that Z2Z_{2} is constant. Necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of an r>0r>0 such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 are given by

    Z0+Z1​<1and(1−(Z0+Z1))2>​4​Z2​Y.Z_{0}+Z_{1}<1\quad\text{and}\quad\left(1-(Z_{0}+Z_{1})\right)^{2}>4Z_{2}Y.

    The two conditions imply that TT is a contraction on the ball ℬ𝒳​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bar{X},r). In order to obtain a small Z1Z_{1}, the operator A†A^{{\dagger}} is conceived as an approximation of D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}) (again based on a finite dimensional approximation of FF). Similarly, the operator AA is constructed as an approximate inverse of A†A^{{\dagger}}, which will then make Z0Z_{0} small. A key point is to define A†A^{{\dagger}} and AA in a smart way, to have good enough approximations while being able to derive tight bounds for Z1Z_{1}. Typically 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a space of functions less regular than 𝒳\mathcal{X}. To this extent, the operator AA acts as a smoothing operator.

  • •

    If the nonlinearity of FF is a polynomial (say of degree dd), Z2Z_{2} can be constructed as a polynomial (of degree d−2d-2), and therefore P⁡(r)P(r) is indeed a polynomial (of same degree dd as FF).

  • •

    All the bounds are obtained through a combination of analytic estimates (because the spaces involved are naturally infinite dimensional) and numerical computations (since they depend on the approximate solution X¯\bar{X}). To ensure that all possible round off errors are controlled during the computations, we use an interval arithmetic package (in our case INTLAB [45]).

As said in the Introduction, this work is far from being the first application of this kind of rigorous computational techniques to solve systems of PDEs, see for instance [5, 13, 16, 18, 22, 23]. Particularly related to our work is the result presented in [10]. In that paper a similar method was used to rigorously validate a bifurcation diagram of steady states of a 3-component reaction diffusion system (without cross-diffusion term). The system considered in [10] depends on a parameter ε\varepsilon and it has the property that its steady states approach the solutions of (4) as ε\varepsilon goes to 00, see  [27]. However, the proof could only be made for a fixed (small) ε\varepsilon and the limit case ε=0\varepsilon=0 is in some sense singular. Therefore the cross-diffusion case could not be handled.

More broadly, techniques similar to the one presented in this work were developed to prove the existence of fixed points, periodic orbits, invariant manifolds and connecting orbits for ordinary differential equations, infinite dimensional maps, partial differential equations and delay differential equations (see for instance [6, 7, 8, 14, 15, 2, 24, 32, 34]). We also mention the existence of comparable techniques where, instead of computing AA by using a finite dimensional truncation as we do, a bound on the norm of the inverse of D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}) is obtained via spectral estimations (see [44, 37] and the references therein). Instead of the contraction mapping principle, computer assisted proofs in dynamical systems are frequently based on topological tools as covering relations, the Brouwer degree, the fixed point index, the Conley index, see for instance [12, 25, 42, 43, 50]. To conclude this paragraph, we refer the interested reader to [3, 4, 21, 48] for a list, surely not exhaustive, of rigorous computational techniques developed to solve a variety of problems, not necessarily in the area of dynamical systems.

Theorem 2.1 is the cornerstone for all the proofs that are presented in this paper. Whatever problem we want to solve, once the system is rephrased as a zero finding problem and the hypothesis of the theorem are verified, then the proof follows as application of the theorem. Thus, for a given problem (𝒫)(\mathcal{P}), we proceed as follows:

  1. 1.

    Introduce a Banach space (𝒳,‖⋅‖𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathcal{X}}) and a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} function FF defined on 𝒳\mathcal{X} so that the solutions of F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 correspond to solutions of (𝒫)(\mathcal{P});

  2. 2.

    Compute a numerical approximation X¯∈𝒳\bar{X}\in\mathcal{X} so that F⁡(X¯)≈0F(\bar{X})\approx 0 and define the linear operators AA and A†A^{\dagger};

  3. 3.

    Define and compute the bounds Y,Zi​(r)Y,Z_{i}(r) satisfying (5)-(8);

  4. 4.

    Check that P⁡(r)P(r) given in (9) is negative for some r>0r>0.

If the last condition is met, the existence of a solution XX for F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 is proved in the form specified in the theorem.

In the sequel we detail each step of the above list for the problem of proving existence of steady states (Section 4) and for the problem of proving their linear instability (Section 6).

3 Sequence space, convolutions and norm estimates

The solutions of system (4) as well as the eigenfunctions of the linearised system are sought in the form of Fourier series, which is fairly natural given the boundary conditions included in (4). This approach also provides a very convenient setting to apply our validated numerics technique. In this section we introduce the sequences space relevant for our analysis and we recall some useful properties. The material presented here is standard and mainly included for the sake of completeness and to fix some notations.

Definition 3.1.

Let ν>1\nu>1. For any sequence u=(uk)k≥0∈ℂℕu=\left(u_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0}\in\mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{N}} we define the ν\nu-norm of uu as

‖u‖ν=|u0|+2​∑k≥1|uk|​ν|k|,\left\|u\right\|_{\nu}=|u_{0}|+2\sum_{k\geq 1}\left|u_{k}\right|\nu^{|k|},

and introduce the space

ℓν1={u∈ℂℕ,‖u‖ν<∞}.\ell^{1}_{\nu}=\left\{u\in\mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{N}},\ \left\|u\right\|_{\nu}<\infty\right\}.

We also define ℓν1​(ℝ)\ell^{1}_{\nu}(\mathbb{R}) the subspace of ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} made of real sequences.

Definition 3.2.

For any u,v∈ℓν1u,v\in\ell^{1}_{\nu}, we define the sequences (u∗v)(u\ast v), (u⋆v)(u\star v) and (u∙v)(u\bullet v) as

(u∗v)k=∑k1,k2∈ℤk1+k2=ku|k1|​v|k2|,(u⋆v)k=∑k1,k2∈ℤk1+k2=ksgn⁡(k1)​u|k1|​v|k2|,(u\ast v)_{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\\ k_{1}+k_{2}=k\end{subarray}}u_{|k_{1}|}v_{|k_{2}|},\quad(u\star v)_{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\\ k_{1}+k_{2}=k\end{subarray}}\sgn(k_{1})u_{|k_{1}|}v_{|k_{2}|},
(u∙v)k=∑k1,k2∈ℤk1+k2=ksgn⁡(k1)​sgn⁡(k2)​u|k1|​v|k2|,(u\bullet v)_{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\\ k_{1}+k_{2}=k\end{subarray}}\sgn(k_{1})\sgn(k_{2})u_{|k_{1}|}v_{|k_{2}|},

where sgn⁡(k)\sgn(k) denotes the sign of kk and sgn⁡(0)=0\sgn(0)=0.

The reason for introducing three different convolution products is that we will deal with multiplications of both even and odd functions. The role played by each of the above operations is as follows.

Let uu and vv in ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} and consider the even functions (still denoted uu and vv) defined by

u⁡(x)=u0+2​∑k≥1uk​cos⁡(k​x),v⁡(x)=v0+2​∑k≥1vk​cos⁡(k​x),u(x)=u_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}u_{k}\cos(kx),\quad v(x)=v_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}v_{k}\cos(kx),

then (u∗v)(u\ast v) is the sequence of Fourier coefficients of the product function u​vuv, i.e.

u⁡(x)​v​(x)=(u∗v)0+2​∑k≥1(u∗v)k​cos⁡(k​x).u(x)v(x)=(u\ast v)_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}(u\ast v)_{k}\cos(kx).

If instead, uu is the odd function given by

u⁡(x)=2​∑k≥1uk​sin⁡(k​x),u(x)=2\sum_{k\geq 1}u_{k}\sin(kx),

then (u⋆v)(u\star v) provides the sequence of Fourier coefficients of the product function u​vuv, i.e.

u⁡(x)​v​(x)=2​∑k≥1(u⋆v)k​sin⁡(k​x).u(x)v(x)=2\sum_{k\geq 1}(u\star v)_{k}\sin(kx).

Finally, if both the functions uu and vv are odd

u⁡(x)=2​∑k≥1uk​sin⁡(k​x),v⁡(x)=2​∑k≥1vk​sin⁡(k​x),u(x)=2\sum_{k\geq 1}u_{k}\sin(kx),\quad v(x)=2\sum_{k\geq 1}v_{k}\sin(kx),

then (u∙v)(u\bullet v) is the sequence of Fourier coefficients of the product function u​vuv, i.e.

u⁡(x)​v​(x)=(u∙v)0+2​∑k≥1(u∙v)k​cos⁡(k​x).u(x)v(x)=(u\bullet v)_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}(u\bullet v)_{k}\cos(kx).

We also recall that ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} equipped with any of the three convolution products ∗\ast, ⋆\star or ∙\bullet is a Banach algebra. More precisely we have the following estimate.

Lemma 3.3.

Let u,v∈ℓν1u,v\in\ell^{1}_{\nu} and ∘∈{∗,⋆,∙}\circ\in\{\ast,\star,\bullet\} any of the convolution products. Then

‖u∘v‖ν≤‖u‖ν​‖v‖ν.\left\|u\circ v\right\|_{\nu}\leq\left\|u\right\|_{\nu}\left\|v\right\|_{\nu}.

Consider now B:ℓν1→ℓν1B:\ell^{1}_{\nu}\to\ell^{1}_{\nu} a bounded linear operator. To the operator BB is associated a infinite dimensional matrix (still denoted by BB) so that (B​u)k=∑j≥0B⁡(k,j)​uj(Bu)_{k}=\sum_{j\geq 0}B(k,j)u_{j} for all uu in ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu}. We denote by \VERT​B​\VERTν\left\VERT B\right\VERT_{\nu} the operator norm of BB, i.e.

\VERT​B​\VERTν=sup‖u‖ν=1‖B​u‖ν.\left\VERT B\right\VERT_{\nu}=\sup_{\left\|u\right\|_{\nu}=1}\left\|Bu\right\|_{\nu}. (11)
Lemma 3.4.

Let B:ℓν1→ℓν1B:\ell^{1}_{\nu}\to\ell^{1}_{\nu} be a linear operator and consider B⁡(k,j)B(k,j) the matrix representation. Then

\VERT​B​\VERTν=supj≥01νj​∑k≥0|B⁡(k,j)|​νk.\left\VERT B\right\VERT_{\nu}=\sup_{j\geq 0}\frac{1}{\nu^{j}}\sum_{k\geq 0}|B(k,j)|\nu^{k}.

A linear functional b:ℓν1→ℝb:\ell^{1}_{\nu}\to\mathbb{R} is a particular case of the general operator BB given above, when (B⁡(v))k=0(B(v))_{k}=0 for any k≠0k\neq 0. The linear functional bb acts on uu as b​u=∑j≥0bj​ujbu=\sum_{j\geq 0}b_{j}u_{j} and the operator norm of bb is then given by , \VERT​b​\VERTν=supj≥0|b⁡(j)|ν|j|\left\VERT b\right\VERT_{\nu}=\sup_{j\geq 0}\frac{|b(j)|}{\nu^{|j|}}. We point out that this last formula is linked to the fact that the dual space of ℓ1\ell^{1} with weight ν\nu is isometric to the space ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} with weight ν−1\nu^{-1}.

When dealing with numerical computations, we need to consider only a finite number of coefficients uku_{k} in the infinite sequence u∈ℓν1u\in\ell^{1}_{\nu}, that is we consider a finite dimensional projection of uu.

Definition 3.5.

Let u∈ℓν1u\in\ell^{1}_{\nu}. For m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} we denote u^m\hat{u}^{m} the truncated part (i.e. the finite mm-dimensional projection) of uu and uˇm\check{u}^{m} the tail part (i.e. infinite dimensional complement) of uu, given as

u^km={uk,k<m,0,k≥m,anduˇkm={0,k<m,uk,k≥m.\hat{u}^{m}_{k}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{k},&k<m,\\ &0,&k\geq m,\end{aligned}\right.\quad\text{and}\quad\check{u}^{m}_{k}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &0,&k<m,\\ &u_{k},&k\geq m.\end{aligned}\right.

By a slight abuse of notation, we also refer to u^m\hat{u}^{m} as the finite dimensional vector (uk)0≤k<m\left(u_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<m}. Moreover, when there is no possible confusion about the dimension of the projection we may drop the exponent mm and simply use u^\hat{u} and uˇ\check{u}.

We end this section with an estimate used to bound a convolution with a tail term.

Lemma 3.6.

Let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and u,v∈ℓν1u,v\in\ell^{1}_{\nu} and ∘∈{∗,⋆,∙}\circ\in\{\ast,\star,\bullet\} any of the convolution products. Then, for all k≥0k\geq 0,

|u∘vˇm|k≤Φkm​(u,ν)​‖v‖ν,|u\circ\check{v}^{m}|_{k}\leq\Phi^{m}_{k}(u,\nu)\left\|v\right\|_{\nu},

where

Φkm​(u,ν)=sup|l|≥m|u|l−k||ν|l|.\Phi^{m}_{k}(u,\nu)=\sup\limits_{|l|\geq m}\frac{\left|u_{|l-k|}\right|}{\nu^{|l|}}.

4 Framework for the existence of steady states

We are now concerned with the proof of existence of non homogeneous solutions of system (4). According to the algorithm outlined in Section 2, the first step is to reformulate the problem in the form F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0, where FF is defined on a proper Banach space. Then we introduce the linear operators AA and A†A^{\dagger}, and finally we provide the definition of the bounds Y,Z0,Z1,Z2​(r)Y,Z_{0},Z_{1},Z_{2}(r). The latter are then combined to define the radii polynomial P⁡(r)P(r).

4.1 Existence of steady states: the function 𝑭\bm{F}

We preventively need to transform (4) into an equivalent system that is more amenable to the application of validated numerics techniques. We introduce further unknown functions and change of coordinates in order to remove the cross-diffusion nonlinearity and to obtain a system with only polynomial nonlinearities (which will be useful when deriving the validation estimates). Then we discretize the obtained system by using Fourier series and finally we introduce FF and the Banach space 𝒳\mathcal{X} in which we look for the solutions.

4.1.1 Auxiliary functions and polynomial system

In order to remove the cross-diffusion nonlinearity we introduce the function ww defined as

w=(d1+d12​v)​u.w=(d_{1}+d_{12}v)u.

Expressing (4) in term of the unknowns vv and ww gives simpler higher order terms, but the nonlinear terms become rational functions. To keep the nonlinearity in the form of polynomials, define the function pp as

p=1d1+d12​v,p=\frac{1}{d_{1}+d_{12}v}, (12)

so that u=p​wu=pw. In term of w,v,pw,v,p, the system (4) takes the form

{w′′+(r1−a1pw−b1v)pw=0,on ​(0,1),d2v′′+(r2−b2pw−a2v)v=0,on ​(0,1),v′​(0)=v′​(1)=0,w′​(0)=w′​(1)=0\left\{\begin{aligned} &w^{\prime\prime}+(r_{1}-a_{1}pw-b_{1}v)pw=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &d_{2}v^{\prime\prime}+(r_{2}-b_{2}pw-a_{2}v)v=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &v^{\prime}(0)=v^{\prime}(1)=0,\\ &w^{\prime}(0)=w^{\prime}(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.

with pp given above as a function of v⁡(x)v(x). However, we want to also treat pp as an independent unknown, on the same footing as ww and vv. For this, it is enough to append a differential equation and some initial conditions uniquely satisfied by the requested function p⁡(x)p(x). Let us consider the equation

p′=−d12​p2​v′,p^{\prime}=-d_{12}p^{2}v^{\prime},

together with the constraint

p⁡(0)​(d1+d12​v​(0))=1.p(0)(d_{1}+d_{12}v(0))=1.

It is straightforward to check that the function p⁡(x)p(x) in (12) is the only solution of such initial value problem. Finally, introducing a variable ss for v′v^{\prime}, we obtain the system

{w′′+(r1−a1pw−b1v)pw=0,on ​(0,1),d2s′+(r2−b2pw−a2v)v=0,on ​(0,1),p′+d12sp2=0,on ​(0,1),v′−s=0,on ​(0,1),p⁡(0)​(d1+d12​v​(0))=1,v′​(0)=v′​(1)=0,w′​(0)=w′​(1)=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &w^{\prime\prime}+(r_{1}-a_{1}pw-b_{1}v)pw=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &d_{2}s^{\prime}+(r_{2}-b_{2}pw-a_{2}v)v=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &p^{\prime}+d_{12}sp^{2}=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &v^{\prime}-s=0,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &p(0)(d_{1}+d_{12}v(0))=1,\\ &v^{\prime}(0)=v^{\prime}(1)=0,\\ &w^{\prime}(0)=w^{\prime}(1)=0.\end{aligned}\right. (13)

to be solved in the unknowns w,v,p,sw,v,p,s. We point out that the usage of the variable pp to recover polynomial nonlinearities is inspired from [33], where this technique was introduced in the context of validated numerics.

4.1.2 Algebraic system in Fourier space

We now expand the unknown functions and we project the differential system (13) onto the Fourier basis. Because of the boundary conditions and (12), v⁡(x)v(x), w⁡(x)w(x) and p⁡(x)p(x) are written as cosine series. On the opposite, since s​(x)=v′​(x)s(x)=v^{\prime}(x), the function s⁡(x)s(x) is expanded on the sines basis. Precisely, consider

w(x)=w0+2∑k≥1wkcos(kπx),v⁡(x)=v0+2​∑k≥1vk​cos⁡(k​π​x),p(x)=p0+2∑k≥1pkcos(kπx),s⁡(x)=s0+2​∑k≥1sk​sin⁡(k​π​x).\begin{array}[]{ll}{\displaystyle w(x)=w_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}w_{k}\cos(k\pi x),\quad}&{\displaystyle v(x)=v_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}v_{k}\cos(k\pi x),}\\ {\displaystyle p(x)=p_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}\cos(k\pi x),\quad}&{\displaystyle s(x)=s_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}s_{k}\sin{(k\pi x)}.}\end{array} (14)

The addition of the s0s_{0} coefficient (which is clearly zero since s=v′s=v^{\prime}) is deliberate, because we see each of the sequence of Fourier coefficients (vk)k≥0\left(v_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0}, (wk)k≥0\left(w_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0}, (pk)k≥0\left(p_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} and (sk)k≥0\left(s_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} as an element of ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu}. Plugging these series expansions into (13) and then projecting back onto the cosine/sine basis, we obtain the following (infinite dimensional) algebraic system

{−(πk)2wk+r1(p∗w)k−a1(p∗p∗w∗w)k−b1(p∗v∗w)k=0,∀k∈ℕ,d2πksk+r2vk−a2(v∗v)k−b2(p∗v∗w)k=0,∀k∈ℕ,−πkpk+d12(s⋆p∗p)k=0,∀k∈ℕ,−πkvk−sk=0,∀k∈ℕ,(p0+2​∑k≥1pk)​(d1+d12​(v0+2​∑k≥1vk))−1=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &-(\pi k)^{2}w_{k}+r_{1}(p\ast w)_{k}-a_{1}(p\ast p\ast w\ast w)_{k}-b_{1}(p\ast v\ast w)_{k}=0,\quad&\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\\ &d_{2}\pi ks_{k}+r_{2}v_{k}-a_{2}(v\ast v)_{k}-b_{2}(p\ast v\ast w)_{k}=0,\quad&\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\\ &-\pi kp_{k}+d_{12}(s\star p\ast p)_{k}=0,\quad&\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\\ &-\pi kv_{k}-s_{k}=0,\quad&\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\\ &\left(p_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}\right)\left(d_{1}+d_{12}\left(v_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}v_{k}\right)\right)-1=0.\end{aligned}\right. (15)

to be solved for the unknown sequences w={wk}k≥0,v={vk}k≥0,p={pk}k≥0,s={sk}k≥0w=\{w_{k}\}_{k\geq 0},v=\{v_{k}\}_{k\geq 0},p=\{p_{k}\}_{k\geq 0},s=\{s_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}.

Notice that because of the equation −π​k​vk−sk=0-\pi kv_{k}-s_{k}=0 with k=0k=0, any solution of this system does indeed satisfy s0=0s_{0}=0. Notice also that for k=0k=0, the equation −π​k​pk+d12​(s⋆p∗p)k=0-\pi kp_{k}+d_{12}(s\star p\ast p)_{k}=0 is an identity. Indeed −0​π​p0=0-0\pi p_{0}=0, and it follows from the definition of the convolution products ⋆\star that (s⋆p∗p)0=0(s\star p\ast p)_{0}=0. In other words, since p⁡(x)p(x) is even and s⁡(x)s(x) is odd, the product s​p2sp^{2} is odd, hence the 00-th Fourier coefficients vanishes. Therefore this equation can be removed and we are then left with a square system.

4.1.3 The 𝑭=𝟎\bm{F=0} formulation

For ν>1\nu>1, we define 𝒳ν=(ℓν1​(ℝ))4\mathcal{X}_{\nu}=\left(\ell^{1}_{\nu}(\mathbb{R})\right)^{4}, where ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} is given in Definition 3.1, and denote by X=(v,w,p,s)X=(v,w,p,s) any element in 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu}. We also use the notation XkX_{k} to denote (vk,wk,pk,sk)(v_{k},w_{k},p_{k},s_{k}). We endow 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu} with the norm

‖X‖𝒳ν=‖v‖ν+‖w‖ν+‖p‖ν+‖s‖ν,\left\|X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}}=\left\|v\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|w\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|p\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|s\right\|_{\nu}, (16)

which makes it a Banach space. We then define the function F=(F(v),F(w),F(p),F(s))F=(F^{(v)},F^{(w)},F^{(p)},F^{(s)}) acting on 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu} by

Fk(v)​(X)=−π​k​vk−sk,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(v)}(X)=-\pi kv_{k}-s_{k},\quad ∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N}, (17)
Fk(w)(X)=−(πk)2wk+r1(p∗w)k−a1(p∗p∗w∗w)k−b1(p∗v∗w),\displaystyle F_{k}^{(w)}(X)=-(\pi k)^{2}w_{k}+r_{1}(p\ast w)_{k}-a_{1}(p\ast p\ast w\ast w)_{k}-b_{1}(p\ast v\ast w)_{,}\quad ∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N}, (18)
F0(p)​(X)=(p0+2​∑k≥1pk)​(d1+d12​(v0+2​∑k≥1vk))−1,\displaystyle F_{0}^{(p)}(X)=\left(p_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}\right)\left(d_{1}+d_{12}\left(v_{0}+2\sum_{k\geq 1}v_{k}\right)\right)-1, (19)
Fk(p)​(X)=−π​k​pk+d12​(s⋆p∗p)k,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(p)}(X)=-\pi kp_{k}+d_{12}(s\star p\ast p)_{k},\quad ∀k≥1,\displaystyle\forall~k\geq 1, (20)
Fk(s)​(X)=d2​π​k​sk+r2​vk−a2​(v∗v)k−b2​(p∗v∗w)k,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(s)}(X)=d_{2}\pi ks_{k}+r_{2}v_{k}-a_{2}(v\ast v)_{k}-b_{2}(p\ast v\ast w)_{k},\quad ∀k∈ℕ.\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N}. (21)

The next Lemma summarizes and justifies in a precise statement all the formal computations and substitutions made previously in this section, with the goal of solving system (4).

Lemma 4.1.

Let ν>1\nu>1. Assume that there exists X∈𝒳νX\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu} such that F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 and consider as in (14) the functions vv, ww, pp and ss. Assume also that the coefficients (vk)k≥0\left(v_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} and (wk)k≥0\left(w_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} are such that the functions vv and ww are positive. Define the function u=p​wu=pw. Then uu and vv are smooth positive functions that solve (4).

Proof.

First notice that since X∈𝒳νX\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu} with ν>1\nu>1, the Fourier coefficients are decaying exponentially fast to 0, and thus the functions vv, ww, pp and ss are well defined and smooth (in fact analytic) 22-periodic functions. Then, having F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 means exactly that the sequences (vk)k≥0\left(v_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0}, (wk)k≥0\left(w_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0}, (pk)k≥0\left(p_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} and (sk)k≥0\left(s_{k}\right)_{k\geq 0} solve (15), which in turn implies that the functions vv, ww, pp and ss solve (13). All the derivatives needed in (13) are legitimate thanks to the exponential decay of the coefficients. Besides, since pp satisfies the differential equation p′+d12​p2​v′=0p^{\prime}+d_{12}p^{2}v^{\prime}=0 and p⁡(0)​(d1+d12​v​(0))=1p(0)(d_{1}+d_{12}v(0))=1, by uniqueness we have

p=1d1+d12​v.p=\frac{1}{d_{1}+d_{12}v}.

Therefore w=up=(d1+d12​v)​uw=\frac{u}{p}=(d_{1}+d_{12}v)u and (u,v)(u,v) does indeed solve (4) (the boundary condition for uu is also satisfied since u′​(0)=p′​(0)​w​(0)+p⁡(0)​w′​(0)=0u^{\prime}(0)=p^{\prime}(0)w(0)+p(0)w^{\prime}(0)=0 and u′​(1)=p′​(1)​w​(1)+p⁡(1)​w′​(1)=0u^{\prime}(1)=p^{\prime}(1)w(1)+p(1)w^{\prime}(1)=0). ∎

4.2 Existence of steady states: the operators 𝑨\bm{A} and 𝑨†\bm{A^{\dagger}}

As outlined in Remark (2.2), the definition of the operators AA and A†A^{\dagger} is based on some approximate solution X¯\bar{X}, which is computed as numerical zero of a finite dimensional projection of F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0.

Extending the notations introduced in Definition 3.5, for X∈𝒳νX\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu} we denote X^m\hat{X}^{m} the vector of truncated sequences, i.e.

X^m=(v^m,w^m,p^m,s^m).\hat{X}^{m}=(\hat{v}^{m},\hat{w}^{m},\hat{p}^{m},\hat{s}^{m}).

Similarly,

F^m=((Fk(v))0≤k<m,(Fk(w))0≤k<m,(Fk(p))0≤k<m,(Fk(s))0≤k<m).\hat{F}^{m}=\left(\left(F^{(v)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<m},\left(F^{(w)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<m},\left(F^{(p)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<m},\left(F^{(s)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<m}\right).

We consider F^m\hat{F}^{m} as acting on truncated sequences X^m\hat{X}^{m} only, so that we can see it as a function mapping ℝ4​m\mathbb{R}^{4m} to itself. Therefore, finding X^m\hat{X}^{m} such that F^m​(X^m)=0\hat{F}^{m}(\hat{X}^{m})=0 is a finite dimensional problem that can be solved numerically. We now assume to have computed numerically a zero of F^m\hat{F}^{m}, denoted by X¯\bar{X}.

The linear operator A†A^{{\dagger}} is defined as an approximation of D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}). However, since we will also need to construct an approximate inverse of A†A^{{\dagger}}, A†A^{{\dagger}} is required to have a simple structure. In practice we impose that A†A^{\dagger} acts diagonally on the tail {Xk}k≥m\{X_{k}\}_{k\geq m}. More precisely, we define A†A^{{\dagger}} (acting on X=(v,w,p,s)∈𝒳νX=(v,w,p,s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu}), as

A†​X^m=D​F^m​(X¯)​X^m,\widehat{A^{{\dagger}}X}^{m}=D\hat{F}^{m}(\bar{X})\hat{X}^{m}, (22)

and

(A†​X)k=(−π​k​vk,−(π​k)2​wk,−π​k​pk,d2​π​k​sk),∀k≥m.\left(A^{{\dagger}}X\right)_{k}=\left(-\pi kv_{k},-(\pi k)^{2}w_{k},-\pi kp_{k},d_{2}\pi ks_{k}\right),\quad\forall~k\geq m.

The operator AA is then constructed as an approximate inverse of A†A^{{\dagger}}. We consider A^m\hat{A}^{m} a numerically computed inverse of D​F^m​(X¯)D\hat{F}^{m}(\bar{X}) and define AA (acting on X=(v,w,p,s)∈𝒳νX=(v,w,p,s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu}), as

A​X^m=A^m​X^m,\widehat{AX}^{m}=\hat{A}^{m}\hat{X}^{m},

and

(A​X)k=(−(π​k)−1​vk,−(π​k)−2​wk,−(π​k)−1​pk,(d2​π​k)−1​sk),∀k≥m.\left(AX\right)_{k}=\left(-(\pi k)^{-1}v_{k},-(\pi k)^{-2}w_{k},-(\pi k)^{-1}p_{k},(d_{2}\pi k)^{-1}s_{k}\right),\quad\forall~k\geq m.

The definition of AA and the fact that ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} is a algebra for both convolution products ∗\ast and ⋆\star (see Lemma 3.3) ensure that A​FAF does map 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu} into itself, as requested in the hypothesis of Theorem 2.1.

Remark 4.2.

To define the action of A†A^{{\dagger}} on the tail space, we simply kept the asymptotically dominant terms of the derivative D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}). Since these terms act diagonally, we are able to easily and analytically invert the tail of A†A^{{\dagger}} and hence to define AA. However, the fact that the dominant terms of the derivative are diagonal is not a mere happenstance, rather it is the result of the various reformulations performed in Section 4.1.1. Had we not introduced the function ww, the Fourier expansion of the cross-diffusion term would create a messy dominant expression that we would not be able to invert analytically.

4.3 Existence of steady states: the bounds 𝒀\bm{Y} and 𝒁𝒊​(𝒓)\bm{Z_{i}(r)}

Having the Banach space 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu}, the function FF, the approximate solution X¯=(v¯,w¯,p¯,s¯)\bar{X}=(\bar{v},\bar{w},\bar{p},\bar{s}) and the operators AA, A†A^{{\dagger}} in hands, we now proceed to derive computable bounds YY, Z0Z_{0}, Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} satisfying (5)-(8) (for 𝒳=𝒳ν\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{\nu}).

4.3.1 The bound 𝒀\bm{Y}

The definition of the bound YY is rather straightforward, and we just consider

Y=‖A​F​(X¯)‖𝒳ν.\displaystyle Y=\left\|AF(\bar{X})\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}}. (23)

The key observation here is that YY can be computed explicitly. Indeed, we recall that X¯∈X^m\bar{X}\in\hat{X}^{m} is a truncated sequence, i.e. X¯k=(v¯k,w¯k,p¯k,s¯k)=(0,0,0,0)\bar{X}_{k}=(\bar{v}_{k},\bar{w}_{k},\bar{p}_{k},\bar{s}_{k})=(0,0,0,0) for all k≥mk\geq m. Therefore we have

Fk(v)​(X¯)=0,∀k≥m,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(v)}(\bar{X})=0,\quad\forall~k\geq m,\qquad Fk(w)​(X¯)=0,∀k≥4​m−3,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(w)}(\bar{X})=0,\quad\forall~k\geq 4m-3,
Fk(p)​(X¯)=0,∀k≥3​m−2,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(p)}(\bar{X})=0,\quad\forall~k\geq 3m-2,\qquad Fk(s)​(X¯)=0,∀k≥3​m−2,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(s)}(\bar{X})=0,\quad\forall~k\geq 3m-2,

and thus F⁡(X¯)F(\bar{X}) only has a finite number of non zero coefficients. This is also true for A​F​(X¯)AF(\bar{X}) (thanks to the diagonal structure of the tail of AA), and therefore ‖A​F​(X¯)‖𝒳ν\left\|AF(\bar{X})\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}} can be evaluated on a computer. To be completely precise, what we mean by (23) is that a (sharp) upper bound of ‖A​F​(X¯)‖𝒳ν\left\|AF(\bar{X})\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}} can be computed using interval arithmetic, and that we define YY to be this upper bound. We are going to repeat this abuse of language whenever we define bounds that involve terms that have to be evaluated on a computer.

4.3.2 The bound 𝒁𝟎\bm{Z_{0}}

In this section we focus on getting a bound Z0Z_{0} satisfying (6). Here and thereafter, when dealing with linear operators on 𝒳ν\mathcal{X}_{\nu}, it is convenient to use a block notation. For a linear operator B:𝒳ν→𝒳νB:\mathcal{X}_{\nu}\to\mathcal{X}_{\nu}, we consider the decomposition

so that, for X=(v,w,p,s)∈𝒳νX=(v,w,p,s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\nu},

and similarly for the other components. Thus, recalling (16) and the operator norm (11),

‖B​X‖𝒳ν\displaystyle\left\|BX\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}} =‖(B​X)(v)‖ν+‖(B​X)(w)‖ν+‖(B​X)(p)‖ν+‖(B​X)(s)‖ν\displaystyle=\left\|\left(BX\right)^{(v)}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|\left(BX\right)^{(w)}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|\left(BX\right)^{(p)}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|\left(BX\right)^{(s)}\right\|_{\nu} (24)
≤ΘB(v)​‖v‖ν+ΘB(w)​‖w‖ν+ΘB(p)​‖p‖ν+ΘB(s)​‖s‖ν\displaystyle\leq\Theta_{B}^{(v)}\left\|v\right\|_{\nu}+\Theta_{B}^{(w)}\left\|w\right\|_{\nu}+\Theta_{B}^{(p)}\left\|p\right\|_{\nu}+\Theta_{B}^{(s)}\left\|s\right\|_{\nu} (25)
≤max⁡[ΘB(v),ΘB(w),ΘB(p),ΘB(s)]​‖X‖𝒳ν,\displaystyle\leq\max\left[\Theta_{B}^{(v)},\Theta_{B}^{(w)},\Theta_{B}^{(p)},\Theta_{B}^{(s)}\right]\left\|X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\nu}}, (26)

where

ΘB(i)=\VERT​B(v,i)​\VERTν+\VERT​B(w,i)​\VERTν+\VERT​B(p,i)​\VERTν+\VERT​B(s,i)​\VERTν,∀i∈{v,w,p,s}.\Theta_{B}^{(i)}=\VERT B^{(v,i)}\VERT_{\nu}+\VERT B^{(w,i)}\VERT_{\nu}+\VERT B^{(p,i)}\VERT_{\nu}+\VERT B^{(s,i)}\VERT_{\nu},\quad\forall i\in\{v,w,p,s\}.

Therefore, we define

Z0=max⁡[ΘI−A​A†(v),ΘI−A​A†(w),ΘI−A​A†(p),ΘI−A​A†(s)].Z_{0}=\max\left[\Theta_{I-AA^{{\dagger}}}^{(v)},\Theta_{I-AA^{{\dagger}}}^{(w)},\Theta_{I-AA^{{\dagger}}}^{(p)},\Theta_{I-AA^{{\dagger}}}^{(s)}\right]. (27)

4.4 Existence of steady States: the radii polynomial

We now collect all the ingredients required to prove the existence of steady states into a unique proposition.

Proposition 4.5.

5 Results about the existence of steady states

In this section we present the computer-assisted proof of existence of steady states solutions stated in Theorem 1.1.

Each solution that is represented on Figure 2 was validated using the procedure described at the end of Section 2. In particular, we computed each solution numerically, implemented the bounds described in Section 4.3, and then successfully applied Proposition 4.5 to validate the numerical solution. By successfully we mean that we found a positive rr such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 and checked that infx∈[0,1]w¯​(x)−r>0\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\bar{w}(x)-r>0 and infx∈[0,1]v¯​(x)−r>0\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\bar{v}(x)-r>0 (with the notation of Proposition 4.5). The numerical data as well as the Matlab codes to perform the proofs and some documentation are available at [9]. To make the computation of the bounds rigorous by controlling round-off errors, the interval arithmetic package Intlab [45] has been used. The computations presented here have been run on a laptop with a processor Intel Core i7 (2.50Ghz) and 8GB of RAM.

Proof of Theorem 1.1. In the script script_proof_branch_steadystates.m fix the values of the parameters r1=5r_{1}=5, r2=2r_{2}=2, a1=3a_{1}=3, a2=3a_{2}=3, b1=1b_{1}=1, b2=1b_{2}=1, d12=3d_{12}=3. The parameter d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d is intended as the bifurcation parameter. Choose a value for the finite dimensional projection mm and a value for the norm weight ν>1\nu>1. Also select a branch of solutions (for the names of the several branches we refer to the documentation and the readme file). The script loads the numerical data, computes the required bounds and verifies the existence of an interval ℐ=(r1,r2)\mathcal{I}=(r_{1},r_{2}) such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 for any r∈ℐr\in\mathcal{I}. If ℐ\mathcal{I} is not empty then the conditions infx∈[0,1]w¯​(x)−r>0\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\bar{w}(x)-r>0 and infx∈[0,1]v¯​(x)−r>0\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\bar{v}(x)-r>0 are checked. In case of successful computation, Proposition 4.5 implies the existence of the solutions. The values for mm and ν\nu that allow the rigorous computation of all the branches depicted in the Figure 2 are available in the documentation.

The script script_proof_steadystate_and_instability.m concerns the existence of steady states for a fixed value of dd. It is used to prove the existence of 13 solutions at values d=0.005d=0.005. Figure 4 shows the numerical data for the 13 steady states solutions. In Table 1 we detail the values for mm and ν\nu used in the proof and the resulting validation radius rr (the script also aims at computing unstable eigenvalues, see Section 7).

6 Framework for the instability of steady states

In this section, we focus on the stability of the steady states whose existence we proved in the Sections 4 to 5. More precisely, we consider the cross-diffusion system (2) in the triangular case d21=0d_{21}=0 and with space dimension one (Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1)),

{∂u∂t=∂2∂x2((d1+d12v)u)+(r1−a1u−b1v)u,on ​ℝ+×(0,1),∂v∂t=d2∂2v∂x2+(r2−b2u−a2v)v,on ​ℝ+×(0,1),∂u∂x(t,0)=0=∂u∂x(t,1),on ​ℝ+,∂v∂x(t,0)=0=∂v∂x(t,1),on ​ℝ+.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}\left((d_{1}+d_{12}v)u\right)+(r_{1}-a_{1}u-b_{1}v)u,\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times(0,1),\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+(r_{2}-b_{2}u-a_{2}v)v,\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}\times(0,1),\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(t,0)=0=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(t,1),\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+},\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}(t,0)=0=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}(t,1),\quad&\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{+}.\end{aligned}\right. (31)

Let (u,v)=(u⁡(x),v⁡(x))(u,v)=(u(x),v(x)) be a steady state of (31). The linearization of (31), around the steady state (u,v)(u,v) yields the eigenvalue problem

{d1ξ′′+d12(v′′ξ+2v′ξ′+vξ′′+η′′u+2η′u′+ηu′′)+r1ξ−2a1uξ−b1(vξ+ηu)=λξ,on ​(0,1),d2η′′+r2η−b2(uη+ξv)−2a2vη=λη,on ​(0,1),ξ′​(0)=ξ′​(1)=0,η′​(0)=η′​(1)=0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &d_{1}\xi^{\prime\prime}+d_{12}\left(v^{\prime\prime}\xi+2v^{\prime}\xi^{\prime}+v\xi^{\prime\prime}+\eta^{\prime\prime}u+2\eta^{\prime}u^{\prime}+\eta u^{\prime\prime}\right)+r_{1}\xi-2a_{1}u\xi-b_{1}(v\xi+\eta u)=\lambda\xi,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &d_{2}\eta^{\prime\prime}+r_{2}\eta-b_{2}(u\eta+\xi v)-2a_{2}v\eta=\lambda\eta,\quad&\text{on }(0,1),\\ &\xi^{\prime}(0)=\xi^{\prime}(1)=0,\\ &\eta^{\prime}(0)=\eta^{\prime}(1)=0,\end{aligned}\right. (32)

where the functions (ξ,η)=(ξ⁡(x),η⁡(x))(\xi,\eta)=(\xi(x),\eta(x)) form the eigenfunction and λ\lambda is the eigenvalue. As announced in the introduction, we aim at proving that most of the steady states obtained in Section 5 are unstable, by showing that the eigenproblem (32) admits an unstable eigenvalue, i.e. there exists a solution ((ξ,η),λ)\left((\xi,\eta),\lambda\right) of (32) such that ℜ⁡(λ)>0\Re(\lambda)>0. The approach is similar to the one used in Section 4: we first reformulate (32) into an equivalent problem more amenable to validated numerics, and then use Theorem 2.1 to prove the existence of an unstable eigenvalue. For this, we again follow the algorithm outlined at the end of Section 2.

6.1 Proof of instability: the function 𝑭\bm{F}

As we did for the steady states, we look for the eigenfunctions (ξ,η)(\xi,\eta) as cosine series. We point out that the steady state (u,v)(u,v) in (32) are non constant functions which have been obtained in Sections 4 and 5. If we directly expand (32) on the Fourier basis, the dominant terms would not be diagonal. We take care of this issue by transforming (32) into an equivalent generalized eigenvalue problem which has an autonomous second order terms.

The two equations in (32) can be rewritten as

M1​(ξ′′η′′)+M2​(ξ′η′)+M3​(ξη)=λ​(ξη),M_{1}\begin{pmatrix}\xi^{\prime\prime}\\ \eta^{\prime\prime}\end{pmatrix}+M_{2}\begin{pmatrix}\xi^{\prime}\\ \eta^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}+M_{3}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}=\lambda\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}, (33)

where

M1=(d1+d12​vd12​u0d2),M2=(2​d12​v′2​d12​u′00),M3=(d12​v′′+r1−2​a1​u−b1​vd12​u′′−b1​u−b2​vr2−b2​u−2​a2​v).M_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}d_{1}+d_{12}v&d_{12}u\\ 0&d_{2}\end{pmatrix},\ M_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2d_{12}v^{\prime}&2d_{12}u^{\prime}\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix},\ M_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}d_{12}v^{\prime\prime}+r_{1}-2a_{1}u-b_{1}v&d_{12}u^{\prime\prime}-b_{1}u\\ -b_{2}v&r_{2}-b_{2}u-2a_{2}v\end{pmatrix}.

M1−1=(1d1+d12​v−d12​ud2​(d1+d12​v)01d2)=(p−d12​u​pd201d2).M_{1}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{d_{1}+d_{12}v}&-\frac{d_{12}u}{d_{2}(d_{1}+d_{12}v)}\\ 0&\frac{1}{d_{2}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}p&-\frac{d_{12}up}{d_{2}}\\ 0&\frac{1}{d_{2}}\end{pmatrix}.

We multiply (33) by M1−1M_{1}^{-1} and obtain the following equivalent formulation for (32):

where the functions (cj)1≤j≤9\left(c_{j}\right)_{1\leq j\leq 9} depend on the steady state (u,v)(u,v) (and on the parameters of the cross-diffusion system), and are given by

Expanding the eigenfunctions in cosine series

Remark 6.1.

Reset of some notations. To maintain the same notations as in Theorem 2.1, we are going to redefine the appropriate 𝒳\mathcal{X}, XX, FF, X¯\bar{X}, AA and A†A^{{\dagger}} corresponding to the eigenproblem (34). Henceforth, we forget about the definition of this symbols that was given in Section 4, and give new ones in the sequel.

For γ>1\gamma>1, we define 𝒳γ=(ℓγ1)2×ℂ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}=\left(\ell^{1}_{\gamma}\right)^{2}\times\mathbb{C} and denote by X=(ξ,η,λ)X=(\xi,\eta,\lambda) any element in 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}. We point out that in Section 4 we could restrict ourselves to real sequences because we were only looking for real solutions, but this is no longer the case here since we may encounter complex conjugate eigenvalues and eigenvectors. We endow 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma} with the norm

‖X‖𝒳γ=‖ξ‖γ+‖η‖γ+|λ|,\left\|X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}=\left\|\xi\right\|_{\gamma}+\left\|\eta\right\|_{\gamma}+\left|\lambda\right|,

which makes it a Banach space. We then fix an index k0∈ℕk_{0}\in\mathbb{N} and define the function F=(F(ξ),F(η),F(λ))F=(F^{(\xi)},F^{(\eta)},F^{(\lambda)}) acting on 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma} by

Fk(ξ)​(X)=−(π​k)2​ξk−(c1∙K​ξ)k−(c2∙K​η)k+(c3∗ξ)k+(c4∗η)k+λ​(c5∗ξ)k+λ​(c6∗η)k,\displaystyle F_{k}^{(\xi)}(X)=-(\pi k)^{2}\xi_{k}-(c_{1}\bullet K\xi)_{k}-(c_{2}\bullet K\eta)_{k}+(c_{3}\ast\xi)_{k}+(c_{4}\ast\eta)_{k}+\lambda(c_{5}\ast\xi)_{k}+\lambda(c_{6}\ast\eta)_{k}, ∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},

F(λ)​(X)=ξk0−1.\displaystyle F^{(\lambda)}(X)=\xi_{k_{0}}-1.

Notice that the only difference between F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0 and system (36) is the equation ξk0=1\xi_{k_{0}}=1. The role of this additional constraint is to normalise the eigenfunction and hence to isolate the potential solutions of FF. Indeed, we can not hope to successfully use Theorem 2.1, which is based on a contraction argument, if the zeros of FF are not isolated. We point out that many different conditions could have been added to isolate the solution, and that this specific choice is rather arbitrary.

We now state the precise link between FF and our stability problem.

Lemma 6.2.

Assume that (u,v)(u,v) is a positive stationary solution of (31) and that there exists γ>1\gamma>1 such that the Fourier coefficients of the functions (cj)1≤j≤9\left(c_{j}\right)_{1\leq j\leq 9}, defined in (35), belong to ℓγ1​(ℝ)\ell^{1}_{\gamma}(\mathbb{R}). Fix k0∈ℕk_{0}\in\mathbb{N} and suppose that there exists X=(ξ,η,λ)∈𝒳γX=(\xi,\eta,\lambda)\in\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}, with ℜ⁡(λ)>0\Re(\lambda)>0, such that F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0. Then the steady state (u,v)(u,v) is linearly unstable.

Proof.

As for Lemma 4.1, the proof just consists in checking that the regularity (i.e. the fact that the Fourier coefficients belongs to ℓγ1\ell^{1}_{\gamma}) of the solution XX and of the data (cj)1≤j≤9\left(c_{j}\right)_{1\leq j\leq 9} allows to rigorously backtrack the manipulations made to obtain FF from the eigenproblem (32). ∎

We point out that the assumption that uu and vv are positive, is in fact only needed here to ensure that pp is well defined. Concerning the assumption on the functions (cj)1≤j≤9\left(c_{j}\right)_{1\leq j\leq 9}, the method developed in Sections 4 to 5 naturally provides us with steady states (u,v)(u,v) for which the Fourier coefficients of uu, vv (and pp) belong to ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu}, for some ν>1\nu>1. However, since some of the cjc_{j} involve derivatives of uu and vv, we can only get that their Fourier coefficients belong to ℓγ1\ell^{1}_{\gamma} for γ<ν\gamma<\nu. We give more details and explicit estimates right below.

6.1.2 About the functions 𝒄𝒋\bm{c_{j}}

The function FF depends on the Fourier coefficients of (cj)1≤j≤9\left(c_{j}\right)_{1\leq j\leq 9}, which themselves depend on the steady state (u,v)(u,v). The method described in Sections 4 to 5 (in particular Proposition 4.5) provides us with an approximate steady state, in the form of Fourier sequences (v¯,w¯,p¯,s¯)(\bar{v},\bar{w},\bar{p},\bar{s}), together with a validation radius rνr_{\nu} which gives an upper bound of the distance (in the ℓν1\ell^{1}_{\nu} norm) between the approximate steady state and the genuine one.

Remark 6.3.

From now on, we denote rνr_{\nu} the validation radius obtained in the computation of the steady states. This validation radius was simply denoted by rr in Section 4 and 5, but this new notation should avoid possible confusions with the validation radius that we are going to consider for the eigenvalue problem.

We now introduce the approximate solution and linear operators needed to apply Theorem 2.1 in the context of the eigenproblem (32).

More precisely, we define F¯\bar{F} by

F¯k(η)​(X)=−(π​k)2​ηk+(c¯7∗ξ)k+(c¯8∗η)k+λ​(c¯9∗η)k,\displaystyle\bar{F}_{k}^{(\eta)}(X)=-(\pi k)^{2}\eta_{k}+(\bar{c}_{7}\ast\xi)_{k}+(\bar{c}_{8}\ast\eta)_{k}+\lambda(\bar{c}_{9}\ast\eta)_{k}, ∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},
F¯(λ)​(X)=ξk0−1,\displaystyle\bar{F}^{(\lambda)}(X)=\xi_{k_{0}}-1, (37)

and ℰF\mathcal{E}_{F} as

(ℰF)k(ξ)​(X)=−(ε1∙K​ξ)k−(ε2∙K​η)k+(ε3∗ξ)k+(ε4∗η)k+λ​(ε5∗ξ)k+λ​(ε6∗η)k,\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{E}_{F}\right)_{k}^{(\xi)}(X)=-(\varepsilon_{1}\bullet K\xi)_{k}-(\varepsilon_{2}\bullet K\eta)_{k}+(\varepsilon_{3}\ast\xi)_{k}+(\varepsilon_{4}\ast\eta)_{k}+\lambda(\varepsilon_{5}\ast\xi)_{k}+\lambda(\varepsilon_{6}\ast\eta)_{k}, ∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},

(ℰF)(λ)​(X)=0,\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{E}_{F}\right)^{(\lambda)}(X)=0, (38)

so that F=F¯+ℰFF=\bar{F}+\mathcal{E}_{F}.

Then, extending again the notations introduced in Definition 3.5, we denote

X^n=(ξ^n,η^n,λ).\hat{X}^{n}=(\hat{\xi}^{n},\hat{\eta}^{n},\lambda).

Notice that the truncation parameter nn does not need to be (and in practice is not) the same as the truncation parameter mm used for the steady states. However, we require n>k0n>k_{0}, so that the isolating condition that we imposed is incorporated in the finite dimensional projection. We also define

F^n=((F¯k(ξ))0≤k<n,(F¯k(η))0≤k<n,F¯(λ)).\hat{F}^{n}=\left(\left(\bar{F}^{(\xi)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<n},\left(\bar{F}^{(\eta)}_{k}\right)_{0\leq k<n},\bar{F}^{(\lambda)}\right).

We consider F^n\hat{F}^{n} as acting on truncated sequences X^n\hat{X}^{n} only, so that we can see it as a function mapping ℂ2​n+1\mathbb{C}^{2n+1} to itself. Therefore, finding X^n\hat{X}^{n} such that F^n​(X^n)=0\hat{F}^{n}(\hat{X}^{n})=0 is a finite dimensional problem that can be solved numerically. Notice that crucially, F^\hat{F} is a finite dimensional projection of F¯\bar{F} rather than of FF, so it only depends on coefficients that are known explicitly.

We now assume that we have computed numerically a zero of F^n\hat{F}^{n}, and denote it X¯\bar{X}. The next step is to define A†A^{{\dagger}} and AA. Again, we are going to take for A†A^{{\dagger}} an approximation of D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}), with a diagonal tail. More precisely, we define A†A^{{\dagger}} (acting on X=(ξ,η,λ)∈𝒳γX=(\xi,\eta,\lambda)\in\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}), as

A†​X^n=D​F^n​(X¯)​X^n,\widehat{A^{{\dagger}}X}^{n}=D\hat{F}^{n}(\bar{X})\hat{X}^{n},

and

(A†​X)k=(−(π​k)2​ξk,−(π​k)2​ηk),∀k≥n.\left(A^{{\dagger}}X\right)_{k}=\left(-(\pi k)^{2}\xi_{k},-(\pi k)^{2}\eta_{k}\right),\quad\forall~k\geq n.

Then, we consider A^n\hat{A}^{n} a numerically computed inverse of D​F^n​(X¯)D\hat{F}^{n}(\bar{X}) and define AA (acting on X=(ξ,η,λ)∈𝒳γX=(\xi,\eta,\lambda)\in\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}), as

A​X^n=A^n​X^n,\widehat{AX}^{n}=\hat{A}^{n}\hat{X}^{n},

and

(A​X)k=(−(π​k)−2​ξk,−(π​k)−2​ηk),∀k≥n.\left(AX\right)_{k}=\left(-(\pi k)^{-2}\xi_{k},-(\pi k)^{-2}\eta_{k}\right),\quad\forall~k\geq n.
Remark 6.6.

As in Remark (4.2), we point out the diagonal dominant behaviour of the derivative D​F​(X¯)DF(\bar{X}) is the result of some preliminary manipulations done on the differential system, in this case the multiplication of the eigenproblem (32) by M1−1M_{1}^{-1}.

The definition of the tail part of AA and the fact that ℓγ1\ell^{1}_{\gamma} is an algebra for both convolution products ∗\ast and ∙\bullet (see Lemma 3.3) ensure that A​FAF does map 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma} into itself as requested to apply Theorem 2.1.

Adopting a similar bloc notation as introduced in Section 4.3.2, we write

A=(A(ξ,ξ)A(ξ,η)A(ξ,λ)A(η,ξ)A(η,η)A(η,λ)A(λ,ξ)A(λ,η)A(λ,λ)),A=\begin{pmatrix}A^{(\xi,\xi)}&A^{(\xi,\eta)}&A^{(\xi,\lambda)}\\ A^{(\eta,\xi)}&A^{(\eta,\eta)}&A^{(\eta,\lambda)}\\ A^{(\lambda,\xi)}&A^{(\lambda,\eta)}&A^{(\lambda,\lambda)}\end{pmatrix},

and define

ΘA(ξ)=\VERT​A(ξ,ξ)​\VERTγ+\VERT​A(η,ξ)​\VERTγ+\VERT​A(λ,ξ)​\VERTγ,ΘA(η)=\VERT​A(ξ,η)​\VERTγ+\VERT​A(η,η)​\VERTγ+\VERT​A(λ,η)​\VERTγ,\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}=\VERT A^{(\xi,\xi)}\VERT_{\gamma}+\VERT A^{(\eta,\xi)}\VERT_{\gamma}+\VERT A^{(\lambda,\xi)}\VERT_{\gamma},\quad\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}=\VERT A^{(\xi,\eta)}\VERT_{\gamma}+\VERT A^{(\eta,\eta)}\VERT_{\gamma}+\VERT A^{(\lambda,\eta)}\VERT_{\gamma},
ΘA(λ)=‖A(ξ,λ)‖γ+‖A(η,λ)‖γ+|A(λ,λ)|.\Theta_{A}^{(\lambda)}=\|A^{(\xi,\lambda)}\|_{\gamma}+\|A^{(\eta,\lambda)}\|_{\gamma}+|A^{(\lambda,\lambda)}|.

Consider 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}, FF, X¯=(ξ¯,η¯,λ¯)\bar{X}=(\bar{\xi},\bar{\eta},\bar{\lambda}), AA, A†A^{{\dagger}} as defined in Sections 6.1-6.2. Now we derive computable bounds YY, Z0Z_{0}, Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} satisfying (5)-(8) (for 𝒳=𝒳γ\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}).

Lemma 6.7.

Define

+ΘA(η)​(‖ξ¯‖γ​ϵ7​(γ)+‖η¯‖γ​(ϵ8​(γ)+|λ¯|​ϵ9​(γ))).\displaystyle\quad+\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}\left(\left\|\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{7}(\gamma)+\left\|\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}(\epsilon_{8}(\gamma)+|\bar{\lambda}|\epsilon_{9}(\gamma))\right). (39)

‖A​ℰF​(X¯)‖𝒳γ\displaystyle\left\|A\mathcal{E}_{F}(\bar{X})\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}} ≤ΘA(ξ)​(‖K​ξ¯‖γ​ϵ1​(γ)+‖K​η¯‖γ​ϵ2​(γ)+‖ξ¯‖γ​(ϵ3​(γ)+|λ¯|​ϵ5​(γ))+‖η¯‖γ​(ϵ4​(γ)+|λ¯|​ϵ6​(γ)))\displaystyle\leq\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}\left(\left\|K\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{1}(\gamma)+\left\|K\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{2}(\gamma)+\left\|\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}(\epsilon_{3}(\gamma)+|\bar{\lambda}|\epsilon_{5}(\gamma))+\left\|\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}(\epsilon_{4}(\gamma)+|\bar{\lambda}|\epsilon_{6}(\gamma))\right)
+ΘA(η)​(‖ξ¯‖γ​ϵ7​(γ)+‖η¯‖γ​(ϵ8​(γ)+|λ¯|​ϵ9​(γ))).\displaystyle\quad+\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}\left(\left\|\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{7}(\gamma)+\left\|\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}(\epsilon_{8}(\gamma)+|\bar{\lambda}|\epsilon_{9}(\gamma))\right).

then

Using the splitting of FF introduced in in (37)-(38) we have

\VERT​A​(D​F​(X¯)−A†)​\VERT𝒳γ≤\VERT​A​(D​F¯​(X¯)−A†)​\VERT𝒳γ+\VERT​A​D​ℰF​(X¯)​\VERT𝒳γ.\left\VERT A\left(DF(\bar{X})-A^{{\dagger}}\right)\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}\leq\left\VERT A\left(D\bar{F}(\bar{X})-A^{{\dagger}}\right)\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}+\left\VERT AD\mathcal{E}_{F}(\bar{X})\right\VERT_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}.

≤‖|A|​|U^n|‖𝒳γ+‖|A|​|Uˇn|‖𝒳γ,\displaystyle\leq\||A||\hat{U}^{n}|\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}+\||A||\check{U}^{n}|\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}},

(c¯1∙K​ξ)=−K⁡(c¯1⋆ξ)+(K​c¯1∗ξ),(\bar{c}_{1}\bullet K\xi)=-K(\bar{c}_{1}\star\xi)+(K\bar{c}_{1}\ast\xi), (42)

‖c¯5∗ξ¯‖γ+‖c¯6∗η¯‖γ+‖c¯9∗η¯‖γ(π​n)2]‖X‖𝒳γ.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\left.\frac{\left\|\bar{c}_{5}\ast\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}+\left\|\bar{c}_{6}\ast\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}+\left\|\bar{c}_{9}\ast\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}}{(\pi n)^{2}}\right]\left\|X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}. (44)

and we provide bounds on ‖A​D​ℰF1​(X¯)​X‖𝒳γ\left\|AD\mathcal{E}^{1}_{F}(\bar{X})X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}} and ‖A​D​ℰF2​(X¯)​X‖𝒳γ\left\|AD\mathcal{E}^{2}_{F}(\bar{X})X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}, for X=(ξ,η,λ)∈ℬ𝒳γ​(0,1)X=(\xi,\eta,\lambda)\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}(0,1). The smoothing effect of AA will make the second bound finite.

First, consider

+(‖ξ¯‖γ​ϵ5​(γ)+‖η¯‖γ​ϵ6​(γ))​|λ|,\displaystyle\quad+\left(\left\|\bar{\xi}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{5}(\gamma)+\left\|\bar{\eta}\right\|_{\gamma}\epsilon_{6}(\gamma)\right)|\lambda|,

Note that explicit upper bound for the ‖K​ε1‖γ\left\|K\varepsilon_{1}\right\|_{\gamma} and ‖K​ε2‖γ\left\|K\varepsilon_{2}\right\|_{\gamma} are required. For this, let γ~\tilde{\gamma} be such that γ<γ~<ν\gamma<\tilde{\gamma}<\nu and use Lemma 6.5 to obtain

≤(ΘA(ξ)​(Υγ,γ~1​ϵ1​(γ~)+ϵ3​(γ)+|λ¯|​ϵ5​(γ))+ΘA(η)​ϵ7​(γ))​‖ξ‖γ\displaystyle\leq\left(\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}\left(\Upsilon_{\gamma,\tilde{\gamma}}^{1}\epsilon_{1}(\tilde{\gamma})+\epsilon_{3}(\gamma)+|\bar{\lambda}|\epsilon_{5}(\gamma)\right)+\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}\epsilon_{7}(\gamma)\right)\left\|\xi\right\|_{\gamma}

=max⁡[max0≤j<m⁡π​jγj​∑0≤k<m|A(ξ,ξ)​(k,j)|​γk,supj≥m1γj​π​j​|−(π​j)−2|​γj]\displaystyle=\max\left[\max_{0\leq j<m}\frac{\pi j}{\gamma^{j}}\sum_{0\leq k<m}|A^{(\xi,\xi)}(k,j)|\gamma^{k},\sup_{j\geq m}\frac{1}{\gamma^{j}}\pi j|-(\pi j)^{-2}|\gamma^{j}\right]

Since FF is quadratic, we have that for all X′∈ℬ𝒳γ​(0,r)X^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}(0,r) and X∈ℬ𝒳γ​(0,1)X\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}(0,1)

+(ΘA(ξ)​(‖c¯6‖γ+ϵ6​(γ))+ΘA(η)​(‖c¯9‖γ+ϵ9​(γ)))​(‖η‖γ​|λ′|+‖η′‖γ​|λ|)\displaystyle\quad+\left(\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}\left(\left\|\bar{c}_{6}\right\|_{\gamma}+\epsilon_{6}(\gamma)\right)+\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}\left(\left\|\bar{c}_{9}\right\|_{\gamma}+\epsilon_{9}(\gamma)\right)\right)\left(\left\|\eta\right\|_{\gamma}|\lambda^{\prime}|+\left\|\eta^{\prime}\right\|_{\gamma}|\lambda|\right)

=max⁡[ΘA(ξ)​(‖c¯5‖γ+ϵ5​(γ)),ΘA(ξ)​(‖c¯6‖γ+ϵ6​(γ))+ΘA(η)​(‖c¯9‖γ+ϵ9​(γ))]​r​‖X‖𝒳γ.\displaystyle=\max\left[\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}\left(\left\|\bar{c}_{5}\right\|_{\gamma}+\epsilon_{5}(\gamma)\right),\Theta_{A}^{(\xi)}\left(\left\|\bar{c}_{6}\right\|_{\gamma}+\epsilon_{6}(\gamma)\right)+\Theta_{A}^{(\eta)}\left(\left\|\bar{c}_{9}\right\|_{\gamma}+\epsilon_{9}(\gamma)\right)\right]r\left\|X\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}.

6.4 Proof of instability: The radii polynomial

We now collect all the bounds developed above into a statement about the stability of the steady states.

Proposition 6.9.

Let ν>1\nu>1. Assume to have computed finite sequences of Fourier coefficients v¯\bar{v}, w¯\bar{w}, p¯\bar{p}, s¯\bar{s} and rν>0r_{\nu}>0 such that there exists a unique (v,w,p,s)∈(ℓν1​(ℝ))4(v,w,p,s)\in\left(\ell^{1}_{\nu}(\mathbb{R})\right)^{4} that solves (15) and satisfies

‖v−v¯‖ν+‖w−w¯‖ν+‖p−p¯‖ν+‖s−s¯‖ν≤rν.\left\|v-\bar{v}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|w-\bar{w}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|p-\bar{p}\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|s-\bar{s}\right\|_{\nu}\leq r_{\nu}.

Choose 1<γ<ν1<\gamma<\nu and let 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}, FF, X¯\bar{X}, AA, A†A^{{\dagger}} be as in Sections 6.1-6.2. Suppose to have computed the bounds YY, Z0Z_{0}, Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2}, defined in (39), (40), (41) and (47) respectively. If there exists r>0r>0 such that

P⁡(r)=Z2​(r)​r2−(1−(Z0+Z1))​r+Y<0,P(r)=Z_{2}(r)r^{2}-\left(1-\left(Z_{0}+Z_{1}\right)\right)r+Y<0,

then there exists a unique zero of FF in ℬ𝒳γ​(X¯,r)\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}}(\bar{X},r). If moreover ℜ⁡(λ¯)>r\Re(\bar{\lambda})>r then the steady state (u,v)(u,v), u=p​wu=pw, is unstable.

Proof.

It follows as application of Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 6.2 ∎

7 Results about the instability of steady states

In this section, we give some details about the proof of Theorem 1.2. We recall that the parameters of (4) are fixed as Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1), r1=5r_{1}=5, r2=2r_{2}=2, a1=3a_{1}=3, a2=3a_{2}=3, b1=1b_{1}=1, b2=1b_{2}=1, d12=3d_{12}=3, and that d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d is left as the bifurcation parameter. For each solution represented by a blue dot on Figure 3, we proved the existence of an unstable eigenvalue, using the procedure described at the end of Section 2. In particular, for each of these steady states we computed numerically an eigenvalue with positive real part, implemented the bounds described in Section 6.3, and then successfully applied Proposition 6.9 to validate the numerical eigenvalue. By successfully we mean that we found a positive rr such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 and checked that ℜ⁡(λ¯)>r\Re(\bar{\lambda})>r. For the steady states displayed previously in Figure 4, we detail in Table 2 what is the value of the unstable eigenvalue, what dimension nn was used for the finite dimensional projection, what γ\gamma was chosen for the space 𝒳γ\mathcal{X}_{\gamma}, and give a validation radius rr for which the proof is succesfull with those parameters (for the steady states where an unstable eigenvalue was actually found).

Proof of Theorem  1.2. In the script script_proof_branch_instability.m fix the values of the parameters r1=5r_{1}=5, r2=2r_{2}=2, a1=3a_{1}=3, a2=3a_{2}=3, b1=1b_{1}=1, b2=1b_{2}=1, d12=3d_{12}=3. The parameter d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d is intended as the bifurcation parameter. Choose a value for the finite dimensional projection nn and a value for the norm weight γ>1\gamma>1. Also select a branch of solutions (for the names of the several branches we refer to the documentation and the readme file). The script loads the numerical data, computes the required bounds and verifies the existence of an interval ℐ=(r1,r2)\mathcal{I}=(r_{1},r_{2}) such that P⁡(r)<0P(r)<0 for any r∈ℐr\in\mathcal{I}. If ℐ\mathcal{I} is not empty then the condition ℜ⁡(λ¯)>r\Re(\bar{\lambda})>r is checked. In case of successful computation, Proposition 6.9 implies that the concerned steady state is unstable. The values for nn and γ\gamma that allow the rigorous computation of all the branches depicted in the Figure 2 are available in the documentation.

The script script_proof_steadystate_and_instability.m concerns the existence of steady states for a fixed value of dd. It is used to prove the existence of 13 solutions at values d=0.005d=0.005. Figure 4 shows the numerical data for the 13 steady states solutions. In Table 2 we detail the values for nn and γ\gamma used in the proof and the resulting validation radius rr. ∎
